newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Prospects seen bright for Bangladesh's National Tubes.
newsitem.headline: Prospects seen bright for Bangladesh's National Tubes.

text.p: Partially state-owned National Tubes Ltd (NTL), which plans to go fully public, has good prospects thanks to an impending expansion of Bangladesh's gas distribution network, brokers and company officials said.

"The government's remaining 51 percent share in the company has been earmarked for selling through the stock exchange in phases," managing director Mirza Khairuzzaman told Reuters at his office in the Tongi industrial zone 10 miles (16 km) from Dhaka.
National Tubes produces galvanised iron pipes for water supplies and pipes for carrying natural gas.

A bridge under construction over the Jamuna river, which will link the capital Dhaka to the country's northwestern region, will carry a gas pipeline intended to plug the north and northwest into the national gas distribution network.

The government hopes to attract foreign investment in the sector and Khairuzzaman said an expected surge in pipe equipment demand following the bridge's completion makes National Tubes attractive to foreign partners.
"The company has immense possibility of tying up with any foreign manufacturer and investor considering the future demand for pipes in the country and neighbouring nations," he said.
Shakil Rizvi, managing director of brokerage Shakil Rizvi & Co., said the company can be expected to gain from a recent surge of foreign investment in the country's gas sector.
Several foreign oil companies including Britain's Cairn Energy Plc are investing in gas exploration. Cairn has found huge gas reserves in the Bay of Bengal.
He said most of the country's gas distribution network had been completed with foreign aid but Khairuzzaman said the increase in foreign investment had created new possibilities in the sector.
"Now I hope to get a slice of that after many foreign companies have started investing in the gas sector," he said.
Bangladesh is under pressure from international donors to privatise state-owned companies, including profitable ones.
The government receives nearly $1.8 billion annually in foreign assistance to finance imports and development and gives about $500 million in subsidies to state-owned companies.

"The company has been profitable since its inception. It only suffered an initial setback in early 1990s because it was exposed to strong competition from imported tubes following the opening up of the country's economy," Khairuzzaman said.
Khairuzzaman said the company supplied 50 percent of market requirements for the pipes.

National Tubes, set up in 1964 in what was then East Pakistan, was nationalised following the country's independence in 1971. The government sold 49 percent of the company's shares through the stock exchange in 1989.
Profit jumped 110 percent to 70 million taka in 1995/96 (July-June) from only 33.2 million in the previous year.
The firm's labour union, however, strongly opposes the government's complete disinvestment of the company.
"Why should we allow the government to privatise the company when it is running profitably?" one union leader asked. ($1 = 43.20 taka)
